exports.9: We still keep three disused frontier posts in a yard by the freight sheds — striped barrier arm, coal stove, and the desk with the stamp still in the drawer. Put one on the far side of the bridge, staffed on Sundays: a crossing is only a crossing when somebody at the end of it asks where you've come from and writes it down.
exports.10: Your residents aren't counting spaces, they're checking whether the town still expects them to come at all. We'll send four masons and the drawings for a stone jetty that runs three hundred metres out and ends in nothing — you park badly at the foot of it, you walk to the end, and you come back with the argument out of you; ours has been settling this exact quarrel since 1861.
exports.12: The port here stopped keeping daylight hours long before anyone thought to ask the mothers about it, and the night room by the customs shed is older than most of our streetlights. We'll send the two women who run 22:00 to 06:00, and more usefully the one iron rule of their rota: the parent coming off shift gets twenty minutes in a chair with a coffee before anybody hands them a sleeping child.
exports.13: Our dockers' side will come over in October and play you honourably, and on the way to the ferry they will take the bell off your pier. Politeness is not the problem — you have nothing you want back.
exports.14: We are a town that made its living insuring ships nobody expected to see again, so: one underwriter, seventy-one, who will write the roof a policy at a premium the council can actually pay and be sincerely astonished if it ever pays out. Beneath him, six lorries of white limestone off the plateau, which has held up every civic building we own, including two that were not supposed to survive the century.

answers.9: Nobody, for about an hour. I take it down to the counter at the café and say it out loud to a man who has heard better news than mine and doesn't look up — then I call my sister, who asks what the catch is.
answers.10: Odessa. Same light off the water, same weather in the afternoon, same civic refusal to be sentimental about which flag is up this year.
answers.12: If both are genuinely fine then it isn't a decision, it's a choice of story. I take the one that will be harder to explain in ten years.
answers.13: The dining room, which we did not eat in. There was a table under a cloth my grandmother ironed on Fridays for guests who came perhaps twice a year, four chairs nobody sat in, and a sideboard with a locked drawer full of paper in three languages — a birth certificate from one country, a school record from a second, a pension letter from a third, all of them the same man. In winter the shutters knocked all night and I would lie on the good carpet working out which of the three I was supposed to be.
answers.14: The Greek church on a Tuesday afternoon. I'm not Orthodox and I'm not really anything, but nobody in there wants a decision from me, and the candle smell hasn't changed since I was nine.
answers.15: Not music — the hiss and knock of a portafilter being emptied. I suspect it follows me because I have almost always just come from a room where it was actually happening.
answers.16: My father's identity card from a state that lasted seven years, folded, unusable, issued by an authority no longer available for correspondence. It proves nothing to anyone now, which is roughly the point.
